bullets: The Ghost does not lecture. It shows Scrooge himself, which is why his reactions (weeping, begging) matter as much as the scenes.
All three scenes are analepsis (flashback), narrated in a warm, nostalgic tone that contrasts with the cold prose of Stave 1.
The order is school (childhood), apprenticeship (youth), engagement (early manhood): a compressed life story.
Fan returns in the present: she is the mother of Fred, so the past is physically linked to Scrooge’s present choices.

core.p: These three characters all appear in the Ghost of Christmas Past’s visit, and Dickens arranges them in a deliberate sequence: first a lonely boy at school who is rescued by love (Fan), then a young apprentice who sees what a good employer can be (Fezziwig), then a young man who loses love because he is choosing money (Belle). The sequence rises to joy and then falls to grief. This matters because it tells the reader that Scrooge’s coldness was not inevitable. Each figure offers him a different route to happiness, and he leaves each one behind.

Dramatic function

Arrives at the empty school to take him home

The Christmas Eve ball in the warehouse

bullets: She says “Father is so much kinder than he used to be”. This implies that Scrooge’s father had been harsh, which gives the reader an explanation for the boy’s isolation without excusing the man.
The triple “home, home, home” is a rhythmic, childlike repetition: it is hope, not a statement of fact.

The Ghost says “she had a large heart” and she “died a woman”; her death is mentioned briefly and sadly, leaving her one child, Fred. The Ghost’s reminder that the child is Scrooge’s “nephew” lands on a guilty, silent Scrooge.
Many critics link Fan with Dickens’s own elder sister, also called Fanny; this is a plausible biographical link but should be offered as a link, not a certainty.
Her presence also quietly corrects Stave 1: Scrooge’s rejection of Fred’s invitation is a rejection of her memory.

callouts.p: She wants nothing from him. Everything Belle later offers is conditional on his choosing her over gold; Fan’s love is the control case that shows what he has given up.

Do not just say Fan is kind. Zoom into the repeated word “home” and say that repetition conveys childish joy and persistence, then explain that Dickens places the Christmas theme of family at the centre of Scrooge’s lost childhood.

core.h: Fan: the sister who rescues him
core.p: Fan appears when Scrooge’s younger self has been left alone at school over Christmas. Dickens uses her to establish the child Scrooge as someone worthy of sympathy before we meet the adult miser in full. She bursts in with joy, kisses him and repeats the word “home” three times, which turns a place into a feeling. Her innocence and speed (she is “always a delicate creature” and yet fearless in confronting their father) show love as active courage rather than softness.

bullets: His wife is “one vast substantial smile”, and Fezziwig himself dances so well that he seems to “wink with his legs”: comic exaggeration that makes goodness attractive, not dull.

The cost of the ball is “a few pounds of your mortal money”, said the Ghost, but its effect on the workers is out of all proportion. Scrooge replies that the happiness Fezziwig gives is “quite as great as if it cost a fortune”.
Scrooge’s “heart and soul were in the scene”: for a moment he is his younger self, feeling, not observing.
At the end he says he would like “a word or two to my clerk”. This is the first time he thinks of Bob Cratchit’s treatment with a flicker of conscience.
The Ghost’s reply is crucial: Fezziwig has “the power to render us happy or unhappy”; employers can make work a burden or a pleasure.
Fezziwig’s name is also comic and generous, in keeping with Dickens’s habit of naming characters to suggest their character.

callouts.p: In 1843 many employers followed laissez-faire ideas: wages and conditions were a matter for the market, not for kindness. Dickens argues that a single employer’s choice can make human lives better, and that good employers are not made poorer by it.

core.p: Fezziwig is Scrooge’s first employer, and Dickens makes him a living argument against cold economics. On Christmas Eve he orders the work to stop early, shouts for his apprentices (“Yo ho, there!”) and has the warehouse cleared for a dance. Dickens turns a commercial space into a festive one through a long, rhythmic list: “snug, and warm, and dry, and bright”. The polysyndeton (repeated “and”) makes the pleasure feel abundant and unhurried, which is exactly Fezziwig’s attitude to life.

head: Fezziwig
Scrooge (Stave 1)
rows: Workplace
“snug, and warm, and dry, and bright”
Cold; the clerk’s fire “looked like one coal”
Attitude to employees
They are people; Christmas Eve is a celebration
Employee is a cost; Christmas is “humbug”
Use of power
Generosity; “a few pounds” buy huge goodwill
Control of money; keeps it all
Result
Loyal workers; joy; remembered with love
Isolation; resented; the clerk is afraid

bullets: She says “You fear the world too much”. Scrooge’s greed is rooted in fear: the shame of poverty, which links to his lonely childhood and to Dickens’s own fear of poverty after his father’s imprisonment for debt.
Her words show agency: Belle takes the decision, spells out her reasons and releases him. She is not a victim waiting to be rescued; she is an adult moral judge.
The release is described as a contract that was “made when we were both poor and content to be so”; the unspoken point is that wealth has made him less content, not more.
She says “May you be happy in the life you have chosen!” The word “chosen” closes off the excuse that circumstances made him a miser.
Later, the Ghost shows Belle years on with her husband and noisy, loving family: a daughter “so like” the girl Belle once was. The warmth of the room is the mirror image of Scrooge’s lonely house.
Belle’s husband says that Scrooge sits “quite alone in the world”. Scrooge cannot bear it and begs the Ghost to remove him.
Scrooge’s outburst (“Haunt me no longer!”) is the climax of Stave 2: he attacks the Ghost, which is a way of trying to attack his own memory.

callouts.p: Do not say Belle left him because she was greedy or angry. The text shows the opposite: she releases him with love, because he has already left her in spirit.
A false god or a thing worshipped in place of what deserves worship; here Belle names the gold as Scrooge’s false god.

core.p: Belle’s scene is the emotional centre of Stave 2, and it is built as a rational, dignified conversation, not a quarrel. She tells the young man that “another idol has displaced me; a golden one”. An idol is a false god, so Dickens is saying that Scrooge has begun to worship money, with religious force. She does not shout or curse; she ends the engagement “with a full heart, for the love of him you once were”. That calm grace makes the loss more painful for the reader and for Scrooge.

bullets: Polysyndeton in the ball (“snug, and warm, and dry, and bright”) imitates the abundance of the party.
Sibilance and soft sounds in the school scenes (“solitary child, neglected by his friends”) create a hushed, pitying tone.
Dickens uses exclamations and dialogue for Fan and Fezziwig (lively, loud); Belle’s speech is calm, measured, formal (a contrast of register that shows her maturity).
Scrooge’s own reactions are narrated: he weeps and grows agitated. This shapes the reader’s response: pity for him rises as his defences fall.

The first small change appears at the end of the school scene: he mutters that there was a “boy singing a Christmas Carol at my door” and he would have liked to give him something. It connects Stave 1 to the redemption of Stave 5.
Narrative viewpoint: Dickens’s omniscient narrator is intimate and chatty, inviting the reader to share the moral judgement.

core.h: Language and structure: how Dickens makes the past powerful
core.p: Dickens’s style changes in Stave 2. Where Stave 1 uses clipped, harsh adjectives for Scrooge, the flashbacks use longer, flowing sentences, lists, repetition and direct speech that sound musical. This shift in prose style is itself a message: memory brings Scrooge’s buried emotions back. Structurally, the Ghost’s scenes are brief, vivid tableaux, so each one has a clear emotional purpose and the reader is led through grief and warmth quickly.

bullets: Sentimental reading: Dickens uses pathos (Fan, the lonely child) to move readers emotionally, and this was a common Victorian technique.
Social reading: Fezziwig is a paternalistic employer, a figure of “Merry England” whose generosity replaces the cold exchange of wages for work.
Psychological reading: Scrooge’s coldness is a defence against the pain of his childhood; the Ghost’s scenes work like therapy.
Moral reading: the past shows free will; each person is shown giving Scrooge a chance, and he chooses gold.
Feminist reading: Belle is one of the novella’s few independent women, speaking with calm authority; yet she is also a figure who leaves the story and disappears into domestic happiness.

callouts.p: Introduce a second reading with: this could also suggest, or an alternative reading is. For example: Fezziwig’s ball could be read as Dickens’s ideal of benevolent capitalism, or as a fantasy that avoids the structural causes of poverty.

core.p: A grade 9 answer does not stop at “these characters are kind”. It considers what Dickens wants the reader to think and feel, and how different readers might respond. Contemporary readers, many of them middle-class householders, would recognise Fezziwig as the kind of employer they could choose to be. Modern readers may see the past scenes as nostalgic and sentimental, or may notice that Dickens offers moral change, not structural change, as the solution to inequality.

callouts.p: Avoid starting with a context paragraph. Weave it in mid-sentence: for example, Dickens’s memory of his father’s debt may explain why Belle accuses Scrooge of fearing the world, since fear of poverty drives the idol of gold.

core.p: Context is only useful when it explains the writer’s choice at a specific moment. For these characters the best contexts are Dickens’s own childhood, Victorian attitudes to work and wealth, and the Christmas traditions he was helping to shape.

head: Context fact
Link to the text

Scrooge’s abandoned childhood; “You fear the world too much” (fear of poverty)
Laissez-faire economics and the Poor Law (1834) dominated attitudes to work
Scrooge’s accounting versus Fezziwig’s generosity
Christmas was being revived as a family festival in the 1840s
The ball and Fan’s “home” are the novella’s model Christmas
Victorian ideal of the home and family as moral centre
Fan’s “home”, Belle’s family scene, Fred’s house
Employers had wide power over conditions; little regulation of clerks and apprentices
Fezziwig’s ball shows power used well; Scrooge’s counting-house shows it used badly

bullets: Short quotations only: “another idol has displaced me” or “quite as great as if it cost a fortune” are ideal.
Make a comparison across the text: Fezziwig and Fred both host Christmas parties; Belle and Fan both offer love that Scrooge refuses; Cratchit as the clerk Fezziwig would have treated well.
For a 6 or 8 mark style paragraph structure: point (idea about Dickens’s purpose), embedded quotation, zoom on a word or device, effect on the reader, context link, alternative interpretation.
Write about Dickens’s methods: contrast, structure, repetition, tone shifts, sentence length and the role of the Ghost as narrator’s tool.
Quote checks: do not quote more than a phrase and do not paraphrase for length; the examiner wants analysis.

callouts.p: Dickens uses the list snug, warm, dry and bright to suggest comfort in abundance, which implies that Fezziwig’s generosity makes even a workplace feel like a home. Replace the list with your own quotation and keep the structure.

core.p: In an extract question on Stave 2 you will analyse how Dickens presents Scrooge’s past through language and structure. In a part (b) question on, for example, family, generosity or regret, these three characters give you quotations you can recall easily. Always make the quotation do work: zoom in on one word (idol, chosen, snug), then explain the effect, then connect to the whole text.

plan: Fan: unconditional love and the lonely child; “home, home, home”; link to Fred in the present
Fezziwig: the abundant ball as an argument about power and employment; the comparison with the clerk’s “one coal”
Belle: the golden idol and the language of choice; why her dignity is crueller than anger
Link forward: Stave 5, Scrooge rediscovers all three virtues; evaluate Dickens’s purpose
essays.q: How does Dickens use Fan, Fezziwig and Belle to show what Scrooge has lost? Refer to Stave 2 and one other part of the novella.
essays.text:
Dickens’s presentation of Fan, Fezziwig and Belle is carefully sequenced to make a single argument: that Scrooge’s coldness was a choice made against three clear alternatives. The Ghost of Christmas Past is not simply showing him sad scenes; it is showing him roads not taken.

Fan’s role is to establish that the young Scrooge deserved love. When the Ghost points to “a solitary child, neglected by his friends”, the adjective “solitary” isolates him on the page as well as in the school. Fan’s arrival is therefore a release, and her triple “home, home, home” turns a place into a feeling, with a rhythm that sounds like a carol. By having Fan say that their father is “so much kinder than he used to be”, Dickens hints at a harsh upbringing, which recalls his own boyhood abandonment in a blacking warehouse while his father was in a debtors’ prison. Yet the more important point is her future: Fan’s death leaves one child, Fred, the nephew whom Scrooge dismisses in Stave 1. The love Scrooge rejected in the present is the love he had once been given.

Fezziwig then shifts the question from love to power. A merchant with an apprentice can be tyrant or benefactor, and Dickens makes Fezziwig the benefactor through abundance. The warehouse is “snug, and warm, and dry, and bright”: four adjectives joined by repeated conjunctions that make comfort seem to overflow. The Ghost’s sarcastic reference to “a few pounds of your mortal money” could be read as a rebuke to Scrooge, but it is also a rebuke to the reader, since in 1843 many employers justified low wages by market economics. It is Scrooge’s answer, “quite as great as if it cost a fortune”, that matters most: he voices, for the first time, a moral calculation that beats a financial one. The structure confirms the shift, because his wish to speak to “my clerk” points forward to the Cratchit household, where the same question of power will be tested.

Belle’s scene is the hinge. She does not rage; she names a metaphor. “Another idol has displaced me” is religious language: Scrooge now worships a false god, gold. The verb “displaced” suggests love shoved aside rather than argued out. When she adds “You fear the world too much”, Dickens offers a psychological explanation rather than a moral condemnation, and the word “fear” turns the miser into a frightened man. Her closing wish that he be happy in the life he has “chosen” closes off every excuse. Perhaps the cruellest effect is structural: the Ghost shows Belle years later with a noisy, loving family, so that the warmth Scrooge forfeited is displayed in front of him until he begs to be taken away.

In Stave 5, the three virtues return in order. Scrooge sends a turkey to the Cratchits, and gives to the charity collector, and takes joy in the family home of Fred, as if repeating the Fezziwig ball on a larger scale. Dickens’s purpose is therefore hopeful as well as critical: the past cannot be repaired, but the lessons it gives can still be acted on.
essays.thesis: Dickens uses three figures from the past not to excuse Scrooge but to prove that his isolation was chosen: Fan offers love without conditions, Fezziwig shows power used generously, and Belle names the exact moment at which gold replaced both.
why: AO1: a conceptual thesis (choice, not circumstance) controls the whole response and is developed, not repeated.
AO2: zooms into individual words and devices (solitary, polysyndeton, displaced, fear) and explains the effect on the reader.
AO3: context (Dickens’s childhood, laissez-faire employment) is woven into analysis of specific phrases.
Alternative interpretation (sarcasm as rebuke to the reader) shows exploratory thinking.
Structural comment links each past figure to a later moment in the novella.

model: Fezziwig is generous: the ball is for his workers on Christmas Eve
Lists and polysyndeton (“snug, and warm, and dry, and bright”) make comfort abundant
Hyperbole and humour (“wink with his legs”, “one vast substantial smile”) make goodness attractive
The Ghost’s “few pounds of your mortal money” shows trivial cost against huge effect
Contrast with Scrooge’s counting-house and Bob’s “one coal”
Context: 1840s attitudes to employers, laissez-faire; Dickens’s own experience of work
exam.q: Starting with this extract (Stave 2, the Fezziwig ball), explain how Dickens presents Fezziwig as a good employer. Refer to the extract and the novella as a whole. (20 marks)
exam.tip: Move from the extract to the whole novella (Scrooge and Bob; Stave 5). Check the marks on your paper; this question tests AO1 and AO2 (and AO3 context, depending on the paper).

model: Belle is loving, dignified, honest: she ends the engagement “with a full heart”
Religious metaphor: “another idol has displaced me; a golden one”
Psychological diagnosis: “You fear the world too much”
Calm register shows her maturity and agency
The later family scene mirrors what Scrooge lost; “quite alone in the world”
His reaction (begging the Ghost) shows guilt and the beginning of change
exam.q: How does Dickens present Belle’s relationship with Scrooge? Refer to Stave 2. (20 marks)
exam.tip: Name the technique and its effect each time. Avoid retelling.

model: She represents unconditional love and rescue from loneliness
“home, home, home” repetition conveys joy and family values
“a large heart” in a delicate body shows moral strength
She explains his harsh upbringing (father) and builds sympathy
She is the mother of Fred, linking the past to the present
Her memory prompts Scrooge’s guilt about Fred
exam.q: Explain the importance of Fan in A Christmas Carol. (8 marks)
exam.tip: Short, focused answer: give three developed points and avoid narrative.

model: Fezziwig as a foil: generous employer versus miserly Scrooge
Contrasting settings: warehouse “snug, and warm” versus cold counting-house
Power can be used to give joy or to withhold it
Fred, Fezziwig and Scrooge in Stave 5 form a pattern of generous hosts
Dickens’s message: wealth only has value if shared; context of 1840s inequality
Structure: the contrast is placed in the middle of the redemption story
exam.q: Write about how Dickens uses contrast to show ideas about wealth and generosity in A Christmas Carol. Refer to Fezziwig and one other character. (20 marks)
exam.tip: Choose a clear comparative thread (hosts, employers, homes) and keep returning to Dickens’s methods.

model: Regret is shown by Scrooge’s reactions: weeping, begging, “Haunt me no longer!”
Belle’s scene makes regret acute: “the life you have chosen”
The Ghost makes him watch, so regret is active, not passive
Stave 4, his own grave and abandoned death sharpen the regret into action
Dickens’s moral purpose: regret leads to reform if acted on
Context: Christian ideas of repentance and a second chance
exam.q: Explore the way Dickens presents the idea of regret in the novella. Refer to Belle’s scene and one other moment. (20 marks)
exam.tip: Use the narrator’s verbs of distress alongside the dialogue.

Para 1: Fan and the lonely child
Para 2: Fezziwig and employer power
Para 3: Belle and the idol of gold

exam.q: Plan: write a thesis statement and a four-paragraph plan for an answer on this question: how does Dickens use the past to show why Scrooge needs to change? (6 marks)
exam.tip: A good plan is a one-line argument for each paragraph with the quotation you will use.

mistakes.r: Analyse what Dickens’s choices achieve: the list, the hyperbole and the “few pounds” contrast, and tie them to the argument about employers.
mistakes.w: Retelling the ball: Fezziwig has a dance, then Scrooge talks.

mistakes.r: Say that Belle releases him because his priorities have changed; she acts out of love, with dignity, naming the “golden” idol.
mistakes.w: Saying Belle leaves Scrooge because he is greedy.

mistakes.r: Explain Fan’s function: unconditional love, the link to Fred, the explanation of a lonely childhood and a harsh father.
mistakes.w: Treating Fan as just a nice sister.

mistakes.r: Weave a single contextual fact into analysis of a specific word, such as the fear of poverty behind “You fear the world too much”.
mistakes.w: Starting with Dickens’s biography for three lines.

mistakes.r: Embed short phrases (a few words) and explain individual words in them.
mistakes.w: Quoting a long chunk of the ball scene.

mistakes.r: Track Scrooge’s own responses (weeping, his “heart and soul” in the scene, begging the Ghost) since they show the writer shaping the reader’s sympathy.
Note that Fezziwig’s importance is that he is not wealthy by miracle but through choice; he shows what Scrooge could have been with the same power.
mistakes.w: Saying Fezziwig is simply good so Scrooge is simply bad.

quotes.a: The Ghost’s description presents the young Scrooge as a victim before he becomes a villain. The adjective “solitary” stresses isolation, while “neglected by his friends” suggests that the loneliness was imposed. This invites the reader to read the later miser as damaged, and plants the idea that Christmas excludes the unloved.
quotes.c: Dickens’s own childhood abandonment in the blacking warehouse.
quotes.q: a solitary child, neglected by his friends

quotes.a: Fan’s triple repetition mimics a child’s breathless excitement and turns “home” from a place into a feeling. Triadic structure makes the phrase musical, almost like a refrain in a carol. It sets up home and family as the novella’s central values, and is a contrast to the empty, dark house Scrooge later returns to.
quotes.c: Victorian idealisation of home and family.

quotes.a: The Ghost’s remark that Fan, though delicate, had “a large heart” is a physical metaphor for emotional capacity. The contrast between a fragile body and a large heart suggests moral strength beyond physical power, and by implication the opposite of Scrooge’s “hard and sharp” nature. It deepens the pathos of her death.
quotes.c: Cult of the loving, self-sacrificing woman in Victorian culture.

quotes.a: This list of four short adjectives, linked by repeated “and”, is polysyndeton that makes comfort seem abundant. The adjectives are all about shelter and light, so the warehouse becomes the opposite of Scrooge’s cold office; the soft consonants and the slow rhythm create a feeling of safety, almost of being held.
quotes.c: Poverty and hardship of working conditions for many Victorian clerks.
quotes.q: snug, and warm, and dry, and bright

quotes.a: Mrs Fezziwig is reduced to a single abstract quality: a smile. The adjectives “vast” and “substantial” are usually used for physical mass, so Dickens makes warmth tangible and fills the space. The hyperbole is comic but also suggests that goodness has weight, in contrast with Scrooge’s thin, withered presence.
quotes.c: Dickens’s comic characterisation and the festive ideal.

quotes.a: The surreal image of legs “winking” celebrates Fezziwig’s lightness and skill, and makes the reader smile. Personification of the legs suggests joy that spreads through the whole body. The humour makes goodness attractive and active; he is generous with energy as well as money.
quotes.c: Victorian popular entertainment and country dance traditions.

quotes.a: The Ghost’s sarcastic phrase shrinks the cost of the party by calling the coins “mortal money”, implying that cash is trivial compared to happiness. “Mortal” also suggests that money dies with us while kindness lasts. It forces Scrooge to measure value in human happiness, not in pounds.
quotes.c: Contrast with laissez-faire ideas that treated labour as a cost.
quotes.q: a few pounds of your mortal money

quotes.a: This is Scrooge’s own defence of Fezziwig, and it is the first time he voices an idea contrary to his Stave 1 creed. The hyperbole of “a fortune” makes the point that kindness has enormous value, and the comparative “quite as great” shows his thinking beginning to change.
quotes.c: The moral economy argued by Dickens against purely financial thinking.
quotes.q: quite as great as if it cost a fortune

quotes.a: Belle’s metaphor uses religious language to frame Scrooge’s greed as worship of a false god. “Displaced” suggests that love has been pushed out of a place, as a person is shoved aside, and “golden” fixes the idol as wealth. Her restraint makes the accusation more painful than anger would.
quotes.c: Christian moral teaching on the love of money.

quotes.a: This short, direct diagnosis reveals the psychological root of Scrooge’s avarice: fear. The verb “fear” turns the miser from a villain into a frightened man, which prompts sympathy. The plain monosyllables show Belle’s gentleness and honesty, and the sentence works as the novella’s central psychological insight.
quotes.c: Dickens’s fear of poverty after his father’s debt imprisonment.
quotes.q: You fear the world too much

quotes.a: Belle’s three words are short, formal and legal in tone, echoing the language of contracts that Scrooge values. She uses his own language to end the bond, and it also shows her control. The act of releasing is an act of love as well as an ending, which is why the scene is so moving.
quotes.c: Women’s limited rights in engagement and marriage in the 1840s.

quotes.a: Reported through the husband’s sympathetic voice, this phrase tells Scrooge what others see: a man isolated by choice. Using the adverb “quite” stresses the totality of the isolation. Its placement in a scene of family noise makes the contrast deeply painful and leads straight to his breakdown.
quotes.c: Victorian belief in the family as the heart of society.

quotes.a: Scrooge’s sudden wish to speak to Bob Cratchit shows the first movement of conscience. The casual, understated phrasing (“a word or two”) shows he cannot yet name his feelings, but the possessive “my clerk” also shows he still sees Bob as his possession. It sets up Stave 5.
quotes.c: Employer duty and clerks’ vulnerability in the 1840s.
quotes.q: a word or two to my clerk

summary: Fezziwig, Belle and Fan are the three figures from Scrooge’s past in Stave 2; between them they show the love, generosity and warmth he once knew, and how his pursuit of money destroyed them.

terms.d: A narrative device that returns to events before the main story; Stave 2 is built from analepsis.
A character who contrasts with another to highlight qualities; Fezziwig is a foil to Scrooge as an employer.
Using many conjunctions in quick succession; “snug, and warm, and dry, and bright” is an example.
Kindness and a desire to do good for others; Fezziwig’s defining quality.
A system where a powerful person (employer) cares for those under him like a father, giving kindness rather than rights.
Language that evokes pity or sadness in the reader; used with Fan and the lonely child.
Using an object or image to represent an idea; the golden idol represents greed as a false religion.
A narrator who knows everything, including characters’ thoughts and the future; Dickens’s narrator guides the reader’s judgement.
